topic.subject: science
topic.title: Force and laws of motion
topic.scope: inertia, balanced and unbalanced forces, Newton's three laws, momentum, action-reaction pairs

misconceptions.statement: If an object is at rest, no forces are acting on it.
misconceptions.why: Students only recognize active forces like pushing and ignore passive forces like gravity or normal force.
misconceptions.fix: An object at rest has multiple forces acting on it, but their vector sum (net force) is zero.

probe.question: A book is lying on a table. What forces are acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No forces are acting on it because it is not moving.

misconceptions.root_belief: What you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: An object needs a continuous force to keep moving at a constant velocity.
misconceptions.why: In daily life, friction always slows things down, making it seem like force is required for motion.
misconceptions.fix: Force is only needed to change velocity; an object will continue moving at a constant speed in a straight line if net force is zero.

probe.question: A spacecraft is moving in deep space far from stars. What force is needed to keep it at 100 km/s?
probe.wrong_answer: A constant force is needed to maintain that speed.

misconceptions.statement: Inertia is a force that keeps things moving.
misconceptions.why: Students treat inertia as an 'internal force' or impetus that an object carries.
misconceptions.fix: Inertia is not a force; it is an inherent property of matter that describes its resistance to changes in motion.

probe.question: Why does a ball keep rolling after you stop pushing it?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the force of inertia is still pushing it forward.

misconceptions.root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Heavier objects have more inertia only when they are moving.
misconceptions.why: Students associate inertia with the difficulty of stopping something, rather than the difficulty of starting it.
misconceptions.fix: Inertia depends only on mass and is present whether the object is at rest or in motion.

probe.question: Does a heavy boulder have inertia while it is sitting still on the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only gets inertia once it starts moving.

misconceptions.statement: Momentum and force are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both terms are used interchangeably in everyday language to describe 'impact' or 'strength'.
misconceptions.fix: Momentum is a state of motion (mv), while force is the agent that changes that state (rate of change of momentum).

probe.question: If a truck has a lot of momentum, does it automatically mean a large force is acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, high momentum means there is a high force inside the truck.

misconceptions.root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A constant force produces a constant velocity.
misconceptions.why: Students fail to distinguish between velocity and acceleration, thinking a steady push results in a steady speed.
misconceptions.fix: A constant unbalanced force produces a constant acceleration, meaning the velocity increases at a steady rate.

probe.question: If you keep pushing a crate with a constant net force, what happens to its speed?
probe.wrong_answer: The speed will stay constant as long as the force is constant.

misconceptions.root_belief: One event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: In a collision between a truck and a car, the truck exerts a larger force on the car.
misconceptions.why: Students believe that the object with more mass or more 'strength' must exert more force.
misconceptions.fix: According to the Third Law, both objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other regardless of their mass.

probe.question: A massive truck hits a small parked car. Which one experiences the greater force?
probe.wrong_answer: The truck exerts a greater force because it is much heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: Bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Action and reaction forces cancel each other out.
misconceptions.why: Students think that because the forces are equal and opposite, they must result in a net force of zero.
misconceptions.fix: Action and reaction forces never cancel because they act on two different objects.

probe.question: If the cart pulls back on the horse as hard as the horse pulls the cart, how can the horse move the cart?
probe.wrong_answer: They cancel out, so the horse must pull slightly harder to start moving.

misconceptions.root_belief: One event has one single target

misconceptions.statement: Passive objects like floors or tables cannot exert a force.
misconceptions.why: Students believe only living things or 'active' machines can exert a push or pull.
misconceptions.fix: Any surface that is compressed or deformed exerts a normal force in response to an applied force.

probe.question: When you stand on the floor, does the floor push up on you?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the floor is just in the way; it doesn't actually push.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only living things can exert force

misconceptions.statement: Momentum is not conserved if the objects stick together after a collision.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the loss of kinetic energy (inelastic collision) with the loss of momentum.
misconceptions.fix: Total momentum is conserved in all isolated systems, even if the objects stick together or change shape.

probe.question: Two lumps of clay collide and stick together. Is the total momentum before equal to the total momentum after?
probe.wrong_answer: No, momentum is lost because they stopped moving relative to each other.

misconceptions.root_belief: Change of form means loss of property

misconceptions.statement: Force is a property of an object that it carries and uses up.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse force with energy or 'oomph' that an object possesses.
misconceptions.fix: Force is an interaction between two objects, not something an object 'has' or 'carries'.

probe.question: When a bowler throws a cricket ball, does the ball carry the 'force' of the throw with it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the ball carries the force until it hits the bat and uses it up.

misconceptions.statement: The reaction force happens slightly after the action force.
misconceptions.why: The names 'action' and 'reaction' suggest a cause-and-effect sequence in time.
misconceptions.fix: Action and reaction forces are perfectly simultaneous; they are two parts of a single interaction.

probe.question: When you kick a ball, when does the ball exert a force on your foot?
probe.wrong_answer: A split second after you kick it, as a reaction.

misconceptions.root_belief: Events in a pair must be sequential
